title: The Decision Room
subtitle: Learn OLAP cubes by solving a retail reporting mystery
audience: Beginners learning OLAP and dimensional analytics

progress.masteryRule: Complete the chapter activity and score at least 80 percent on its quiz; retries are unlimited.

chapters.title: Enter the Decision Room
chapters.objective: Understand why OLTP and OLAP solve different problems.
chapters.story: Three Northstar reports disagree. Mira asks you to identify which questions belong to transaction systems and which belong to analytical systems.
concepts: OLTP records individual business events.
OLAP compares and summarizes many events.
A cube may have more than three dimensions.

interaction.instruction: Answer all six questions by sorting each one into Run the business now or Understand the business over time.

chapters.debrief: OLTP captures events; OLAP turns many events into comparable evidence.

quiz.question: Which system is optimized for recording one order?
quiz.explanation: OLTP handles small, frequent transaction writes.

quiz.question: Which system is optimized for comparing years and regions?
quiz.explanation: OLAP scans and summarizes many records.

quiz.question: An OLAP cube must always have exactly three dimensions.
quiz.explanation: The cube drawing is a mental model; real analytical models can have many dimensions.

chapters.title: Read the Raw Evidence
chapters.objective: Follow keys across raw customers, products, stores, orders, and order lines.
chapters.story: Mira gives you the source tables and warns that an order header is not the same thing as a sold item.
concepts: A primary key identifies one row.
A foreign key connects related rows.
Order headers and order lines have different grains.

interaction.instruction: Select an order and follow its customer, store, and product lines.
interaction.completion: Trace order 1002 and inspect cancelled order 1006.

chapters.debrief: Before aggregating, follow the keys and understand what one row means.

quiz.question: Where is product quantity stored?
quiz.explanation: Each order-line row records a product and its quantity.

quiz.question: Why can one order appear on several order-line rows?
quiz.explanation: One order can contain multiple products.

quiz.question: Should cancelled order 1006 count toward completed net sales?
quiz.explanation: Its source status is cancelled, so it must be excluded from completed facts.

chapters.title: Define One Fact
chapters.objective: Declare the fact grain before selecting measures.
chapters.story: An early report repeats order totals on every line and counts sales twice.
concepts: Grain states exactly what one fact row means.
The chosen grain is one product line on one completed order.
Mixing grains creates duplication.

interaction.instruction: Inspect the order, order-line, and product-per-day grain choices, then choose one completed order line.
interaction.completion: Choose one completed order line and pass the UNIQUE(order_id, line_no) duplication check.

chapters.debrief: Grain is the contract that keeps every number honest.

quiz.question: What should be decided before selecting measures?
quiz.explanation: Measures must match the exact meaning of one row.

quiz.question: Can an order total be repeated on every line and safely summed?
quiz.explanation: Repeating a header total at line grain causes double-counting.

quiz.question: What does one practice fact row describe?
quiz.explanation: The declared grain is one product line on one completed order.

chapters.title: Build the Star
chapters.objective: Arrange facts and dimensions into a simple star schema.
chapters.story: The operational tables work for order entry but make repeated analysis difficult.
concepts: The fact table stores measurable events.
Dimensions describe facts.
A star schema surrounds one central fact table with dimensions.

interaction.instruction: Place each field in Fact Sales or the correct dimension, then connect every fact key to its dimension.
interaction.completion: Place all eight fields correctly and connect all four fact keys.

chapters.debrief: The star makes common analytical joins predictable.

quiz.question: Where does net_amount belong?
quiz.explanation: Net amount measures each sales fact.

quiz.question: Where does category belong?
quiz.explanation: Category describes a product.

quiz.question: Why is it called a star schema?
options: Dimensions surround a central fact table
quiz.explanation: Its common diagram resembles a star.

chapters.title: Describe the Business
chapters.objective: Use dimensions, members, levels, attributes, and hierarchies correctly.
chapters.story: The star has tables, but the team needs shared words for navigating them.
concepts: A dimension is an analysis angle.
A member is one value in a dimension.
A hierarchy orders levels from broad to detailed.

interaction.instruction: Choose the valid Time and Store ladders from detailed members toward the All member.
interaction.completion: Complete Day → Month → Quarter → Year → All and Store → Region → All.

chapters.debrief: Dimensions provide coordinates; hierarchies provide routes between detail levels.

quiz.question: In Year → Quarter → Month, what is Quarter?
quiz.explanation: Quarter is one level in the Time hierarchy.

quiz.question: In the Store dimension, what is South?
quiz.explanation: South is one member value.

quiz.question: What enables consistent roll-up and drill-down?
quiz.explanation: A hierarchy defines the ordered levels.

chapters.title: Choose Measures Carefully
chapters.objective: Know when a measure can be summed and when it must be recalculated.
chapters.story: A dashboard adds percentages and produces a number that has no useful meaning.
concepts: Additive measures sum across dimensions.
Semi-additive measures have limits, often across time.
Ratios should usually be recalculated from aggregated components.

interaction.instruction: Classify all seven measures as Safe to sum, Recalculate from parts, or Do not sum across time.

chapters.debrief: The aggregation rule is part of a measure's definition.

quiz.question: Is net sales additive in this dataset?
quiz.explanation: Net sales can be summed across the displayed dimensions.

quiz.question: Should monthly margin percentages be added to get a quarter margin?
quiz.explanation: Percentages are non-additive.

quiz.question: How should quarter average selling price be found?
options: Aggregate sales and units, then divide
quiz.explanation: Recomputing from components preserves weighting.

chapters.title: Create the First Cube
chapters.objective: Read a Month × Region × Category cube and inspect its cells.
chapters.story: You turn completed facts into a view leaders can explore by business coordinates.
concepts: A cell is identified by one member from each displayed dimension.
The cell stores an aggregated measure.
Missing does not automatically mean zero.

interaction.instruction: Choose Month, Region, and Category coordinates and inspect the contributing facts.
interaction.completion: Find three populated cells and one missing cell.

chapters.debrief: A cube navigates grouped facts using business coordinates.

quiz.question: What is the measure in the practice cube?
quiz.explanation: Net sales is aggregated in each cell.

quiz.question: What identifies one cube cell?
options: One member from every displayed dimension
quiz.explanation: The member combination forms the coordinate.

quiz.question: Does a blank March cell prove sales were zero?
quiz.explanation: It may mean no matching fact was recorded.

chapters.title: Ask with SQL
chapters.objective: Connect joins, filters, grouping, and aggregation to the visual cube.
chapters.story: Mira asks for a reproducible query behind every displayed answer.
concepts: JOIN attaches dimension descriptions.
WHERE filters rows before aggregation.
GROUP BY defines result groups and SUM computes the measure.

interaction.instruction: Arrange SELECT, FROM and JOIN, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, and ORDER BY blocks.
interaction.completion: Build and run the Month × Region × Category query.

chapters.debrief: SQL makes the cube's grouping logic visible and repeatable.

quiz.question: Which clause creates Month × Region × Category groups?
quiz.explanation: GROUP BY defines each result group.

quiz.question: Which clause removes rows before aggregation?
quiz.explanation: WHERE filters source rows.

quiz.question: Which clause can keep only groups above ₹2,000?
quiz.explanation: HAVING filters after grouping.

chapters.title: Slice and Dice
chapters.objective: Focus a cube with one-member and multi-member filters.
chapters.story: A manager first asks for February only, then for a small comparison across several dimensions.
concepts: Slice fixes one dimension to one member.
Dice chooses ranges or sets across multiple dimensions.
Active filters should remain visible.

interaction.instruction: Create the February slice and then the Jan/Feb, South/West, Apparel dice.

chapters.debrief: Slice focuses one coordinate; dice selects a smaller multidimensional region.

quiz.question: Only February is which operation?
quiz.explanation: It fixes the Time dimension to one member.

quiz.question: Jan or Feb, South or West, Apparel only is which operation?
quiz.explanation: It selects sets across several dimensions.

quiz.question: Does dice require a literal three-dimensional cube?
quiz.explanation: The operation applies to multidimensional analysis with any practical number of dimensions.

chapters.title: Roll Up and Drill Down
chapters.objective: Move between summary and detail levels without losing reconciliation.
chapters.story: Leadership begins with Q1 and asks which months created the result.
concepts: Roll-up moves to a broader hierarchy level.
Drill-down moves to a more detailed level.
Totals should reconcile for additive measures.

interaction.instruction: Move between Day, Month, Quarter, and Year while watching facts combine or separate.
interaction.completion: Visit all four levels, then complete Month → Quarter → Month while observing January, February, and the missing March member roll into Q1.

chapters.debrief: Roll-up changes the level of detail; drill-down reveals contributors.

quiz.question: Month → Quarter is what?
quiz.explanation: Quarter is the broader level.

quiz.question: Quarter → Month is what?
quiz.explanation: Month is the more detailed level.

quiz.question: Should Q1 equal its displayed months for net sales?
quiz.explanation: Net sales is additive here, so the levels must reconcile.

chapters.title: Pivot and Drill Through
chapters.objective: Rotate a result and open the fact evidence behind one cell.
chapters.story: One manager wants regions in columns while Finance wants to inspect the source lines.
concepts: Pivot changes presentation, not facts.
Drill-through opens detailed fact records.
Drill-through differs from moving down a hierarchy.

interaction.instruction: Swap rows and columns, then open February × North × Home.
interaction.completion: Verify that the rotated total is unchanged and the two fact rows sum to ₹6,600.

chapters.debrief: Pivot changes viewpoint; drill-through exposes evidence.

quiz.question: Does pivot change net sales?
quiz.explanation: It only rotates how the same result is displayed.

quiz.question: What opens the fact rows behind ₹6,600?
quiz.explanation: Drill-through reveals the underlying records.

quiz.question: Is drill-through the same as Month → Day?
quiz.explanation: Month to Day is hierarchy drill-down; drill-through opens source facts.

chapters.title: Ask for Every Subtotal
chapters.objective: Understand CUBE, ROLLUP, GROUPING SETS, and subtotal labels.
chapters.story: The executive table needs detail rows, several subtotals, and a grand total together.
concepts: CUBE creates every grouping combination.
ROLLUP follows hierarchical prefixes.
GROUPING SETS explicitly lists desired groupings.

interaction.instruction: Generate the three-dimension CUBE, classify all eight grouping patterns, and compare CUBE, ROLLUP, and GROUPING SETS.
interaction.completion: Classify all eight patterns correctly and visit all three subtotal operators.

chapters.debrief: SQL cube operators coordinate detail, subtotal, and grand-total views.

quiz.question: How many grouping patterns can a full CUBE create for three dimensions?
quiz.explanation: Each dimension is either included or rolled up, so there are 2³ patterns.

quiz.question: Which construct explicitly names only wanted combinations?
quiz.explanation: GROUPING SETS lists the exact groupings.

quiz.question: Why label subtotal NULL values?
options: To distinguish all members from missing data
quiz.explanation: Subtotal markers and genuine missing values must not be confused.

chapters.title: Avoid Analytical Traps
chapters.objective: Diagnose joins, filters, ratios, and missing-value errors.
chapters.story: You review four reports that look reasonable but give wrong answers.
concepts: Fan-out joins duplicate facts.
No row is not automatically zero.
Ratios should be recomputed at the requested level.

interaction.instruction: Inspect each symptom and its stated cause, then choose the repair that removes the error.
interaction.completion: Choose the correct repair for all four analytical-error cases.

chapters.debrief: A fast wrong cube is still wrong; correctness starts with data meaning.

quiz.question: What proves a dimension join is safe?
options: One valid matching dimension row per fact key version
quiz.explanation: A non-unique match can duplicate each fact.

quiz.question: Is no row automatically equal to zero?
quiz.explanation: Missing observation and measured zero are different claims.

quiz.question: Why is average of averages risky?
quiz.explanation: Groups with different weights should not count equally.

chapters.title: Choose an OLAP Engine
chapters.objective: Compare ROLAP, MOLAP, and HOLAP trade-offs.
chapters.story: Northstar must choose where detailed facts and aggregates should live.
concepts: ROLAP analyzes relational facts with SQL.
MOLAP emphasizes precomputed multidimensional structures.
HOLAP combines relational detail and multidimensional aggregates.

interaction.instruction: Try all three scenario presets and observe how size, freshness, speed, and detail needs change the suggested engine family.
interaction.completion: Try all three presets and observe the ROLAP, MOLAP, and HOLAP recommendations.

chapters.debrief: Engine choice balances freshness, scale, speed, storage, and detail access.

quiz.question: Which approach keeps detailed facts mainly in relational tables?
quiz.explanation: ROLAP uses relational storage and SQL.

quiz.question: Which approach emphasizes precomputed multidimensional storage?
quiz.explanation: MOLAP processes data into multidimensional structures.

quiz.question: Which approach combines relational detail and multidimensional aggregates?
quiz.explanation: HOLAP is the hybrid approach.

chapters.title: Make It Fast and Trustworthy
chapters.objective: Apply performance techniques and data-quality checks.
chapters.story: The result is correct, but the query is slow and the daily refresh sometimes arrives late.
concepts: Partitioning and columnar storage reduce work.
Precomputed aggregates speed repeated questions.
Quality checks protect grain, keys, freshness, and reconciliation.
The deterministic lab freshness time is 2026-04-30 06:00 UTC.

interaction.instruction: Apply one performance control and run all Northstar data checks.
interaction.completion: Reach green status for fact count, keys, balance, totals, and freshness.

chapters.debrief: Performance earns attention; quality earns trust.

quiz.question: What reduces scanning when queries filter by date?
quiz.explanation: Partition pruning avoids unrelated dates.

quiz.question: What keeps net sales defined once for every dashboard?
options: A governed metric or semantic layer
quiz.explanation: A shared definition prevents metric drift.

quiz.question: What should happen if a checksum fails?
options: Stop or quarantine the refresh and investigate
quiz.explanation: Bad data should not silently reach users.

chapters.title: Leadership Review
chapters.objective: Build a traceable Decision Brief from model choices, SQL, and evidence.
chapters.story: You must settle the disagreement and present one defensible conclusion to Northstar leadership.
concepts: Every claim needs a clear metric and filter.
Aggregate totals must reconcile.
Drill-through and SQL connect the answer to evidence.

interaction.instruction: Choose a defensible claim, reproducible query, drill-through evidence, coverage caveat, and recommendation.
interaction.completion: Select the correct five cards to produce and save the complete Decision Brief.

chapters.debrief: A trustworthy answer connects business meaning, model design, calculation, and source evidence.

quiz.question: Which design decision protects every later total?
quiz.explanation: Grain defines what is safe to count and sum.

quiz.question: Which operation produced the Q1 summary from months?
quiz.explanation: Month to Quarter is a roll-up.

quiz.question: What proves where one aggregate came from?
quiz.explanation: The detailed facts and query provide traceable evidence.

quiz.question: What is Northstar's trusted completed net-sales total?
quiz.explanation: ₹19,800 is gross ₹21,150 minus discounts ₹1,350, excluding cancelled order 1006.

chapters.title: Close the Case and Choose the Next Mission
chapters.objective: Connect the complete OLAP mental model, state the conclusions, and choose a further-learning path.
chapters.story: Leadership accepts the Decision Brief. Mira asks you to rebuild the idea from memory and choose your next mission.
concepts: Events become declared-grain facts.
Facts connect to dimensions and hierarchies.
Defined measures form cube cells that can be navigated and verified.

interaction.instruction: Arrange the eight-stage OLAP chain, match every operation, and select a next learning path.
interaction.completion: Complete the map, recap board, and one next-mission checklist.

chapters.debrief: Trustworthy analysis begins with clear meaning, becomes useful through multidimensional exploration, and stays trustworthy through reproducible evidence.

quiz.question: What must be clear before building aggregates?
quiz.explanation: Aggregation cannot repair an ambiguous row or metric.

quiz.question: Which structures describe how a fact can be grouped?
quiz.explanation: Dimensions are analysis angles and hierarchies organize their levels.

quiz.question: Which operation changes table orientation without changing facts?
quiz.explanation: Pivot rotates presentation.

quiz.question: What is the strongest way to prove an aggregate?
options: Reproduce it with SQL and drill through to facts
quiz.explanation: Reproducible calculation plus source evidence makes the result traceable.

quiz.question: Every OLAP system uses the same physical storage.
quiz.explanation: The concepts apply across different relational, multidimensional, hybrid, and modern architectures.
